unit.title: Number and Calculation
unit.blurb: Rational and irrational numbers, estimating roots, standard form for very large and very small numbers, and the laws of indices.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Tell rational numbers from irrational numbers and explain why a number is irrational.

O2.t: Estimate square roots and cube roots, and say which two whole numbers a surd lies between.

O3.t: Write and order numbers in standard form, and calculate with numbers in standard form.

O4.t: Use positive, zero and negative indices and the laws of indices for multiplication, division and powers.

p: A **rational number** can be written as a fraction a/b where a and b are integers and b is not 0. Every integer, every fraction, every terminating decimal (0.375 = 3/8) and every recurring decimal (0.333… = 1/3) is rational.
An **irrational number** cannot be written as a fraction. Its decimal goes on for ever **without repeating**. Examples: √2 = 1.41421356…, √10, ∛5 and π = 3.14159…

The square root of a whole number is rational only if the number is a **square number**: √49 = 7 is rational, √50 is irrational. In the same way, a cube root of a whole number is rational only for cube numbers.
Ask: can it be written exactly as a fraction of two integers?
steps: √n with n a square number, ∛n with n a cube?

p: To find the two whole numbers a root lies between, find the **square numbers either side**. 40 lies between 36 and 49, so √40 lies between √36 = 6 and √49 = 7.
√40 is closer to 6 than to 7, because 40 is much closer to 36 than to 49. A good estimate is about 6.3.

steps: find the cube numbers either side of 90

p: Every fraction becomes a decimal that stops or repeats. √2 = 1.41421356… never stops and never repeats, so it cannot be written as a fraction: it is irrational.
√n is rational only when n is a square number (√49 = 7); otherwise it is irrational.
√50 is NOT 25. A square root asks which number multiplied by ITSELF gives 50. 7 × 7 = 49, so √50 is just over 7.

p: A number in **standard form** is written **A × 10ⁿ** where **1 ≤ A < 10** and n is an integer.
Large numbers have a positive power: 4 300 000 = 4.3 × 10⁶ (the decimal point moves 6 places).
Small numbers have a negative power: 0.000 072 = 7.2 × 10⁻⁵ (the point moves 5 places to the right, so the power is −5).

steps: put the point after the first non-zero digit
moving right means a negative power

p: Multiply: multiply the A parts and **add** the powers. Divide: divide the A parts and **subtract** the powers. Then make sure A is between 1 and 10.

23 × 10⁴ is NOT standard form. Write 23 as 2.3 × 10¹ and add the powers: 2.3 × 10⁵.

p: For any number a (not 0): **aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ**, **aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ** and **(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ**.
These laws only work when the **base is the same**: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷, but 2³ × 3⁴ cannot be combined this way.
Dividing a power by itself gives 1, so **a⁰ = 1**.
A negative index means 'one over': **a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ**. So 5⁻² = 1/25 and 10⁻³ = 1/1000 = 0.001.

p: Divide powers: 2³ ÷ 2⁵ = 2⁻². But also 8 ÷ 32 = 1/4 = 1/2². So 2⁻² must equal 1/2².
A negative index means 'one over': a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. It does not make the number negative.
2³ × 2⁴ is 2⁷, NOT 4⁷. The base stays the same; only the indices change.
